Q: Leslie Matrix Simulation Coding A:

your code needs some adjustments to make it working: master_results needs to be initialized with the correct length and given names to assign the results; the last } was missing, and master_results needs to be moved to be the last statement of the function: that is what R returns.

I also added argument 'stoch': 'stochastic_multiplier' is set to 1 if 'stoch' is FALSE, so the only remaining stochasticity is the initialization of the number of females between 'Init_Min' and 'Init_Max'. Running with stoch = FALSE makes it easier to see what is going on for a first check.

I also added code to run the different scenarios and generate plots to compare them:

#### Loading packages ####
library(ggplot2)


#### Setting the seed ####
set.seed(314, kind = "default", normal.kind = "default", sample.kind = "default")


#### DEFINE PARAMETERS ####
harvest_levels <- c(31, 39, 77, 155) # number of females harvested annually
#out of 80, 100, 200, 400 total harvest
# assuming females are 39% of harvest
# 31 is current, assuming 80 animals harvested per year

nSims <- 25 # was 1000
nYears <- 50
Init_Min <- 2222 # min initial population
Init_Max <- 3965 # max initial population

SAD_Split <- c(0.67, 0.33) # assumed stable age distribution, we are assuming this from harvest
harvest_weights <- c(0.67, 0.33) # weight of harvest, same as SAD (Juveniles, adults)

# Density dependence
K_total <- 4000
K_females <- K_total * 0.39

# DEFINE BASE MATRICES
# Butterflies and Rainbows Matrix
bfar_mat <- matrix(c(0, # female offspring per juvenile
                     0.82, #female offspring per adult female
                     0.48, # juvenile survival Loforth et al. 2023
                     0.82), # Adult survival Loforth et al. 2023
                   nrow=2, byrow=T)
# Doom and Gloom Matrix
dag_mat <- matrix(c(0, # female offspring per juvenile
                    0.374, #female offspring per adult female
                    0.27, # juvenile survival Paragi et al. 1994
                    0.65), # Adult survival Paragi et al. 1994
                  nrow=2, byrow=T)
# Alternative Doom and Gloom
adag_mat <- matrix(c(0,
                     0.374, # same as doom and gloom
                     0.83, # juvenile survival Kuntze et al. 2024
                     0.82), # adult survival Kuntze et al. 2024
                   nrow=2, byrow=T)

#### CREATE FUNCTION ####
run_leslie_loop <- function(base_mat = bfar_mat,
                            harvest_levels = harvest_levels,
                            stoch = TRUE,
                            nSims = nSims,
                            nYears = nYears,
                            Init_Min = Init_Min,
                            Init_Max = Init_Max,
                            K_females = K_females,
                            SAD_Split = SAD_Split,
                            harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                            scenario_name) {

  # Pre-calculate growth rate
  ev <- eigen(base_mat)
  R_growth <- max(Re(ev$values))

  master_results <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(harvest_levels)) # Was: master_results <- list()
  names(master_results) <- as.character(harvest_levels) # I added this

  # Loop over harvest levels
  for (h in harvest_levels) {

    sim_results <- vector("list", nSims)
    current_h_vec <- h * harvest_weights

    # Simulation loop
    for (s in 1:nSims) {

      allYears <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = nYears + 1)

      # Random starting population
      Rand_Start_Females <- runif(1, Init_Min, Init_Max) * 0.39
      allYears[, 1] <- Rand_Start_Females * SAD_Split

      for (t in 2:(nYears + 1)) {

        # Stochasticity
        if(stoch == TRUE) {
          stochastic_multiplier <- rlnorm(1, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 0.1)
        } else {
          stochastic_multiplier <- 1
        }
        current_mat <- base_mat * stochastic_multiplier

        N_before <- current_mat %*% allYears[, t - 1]

        # Density dependence (Beverton-Holt)
        N_curr <- sum(allYears[, t - 1])
        dd <- 1 + ((R_growth - 1) * N_curr / K_females)

        N_after <- N_before / dd

        # Harvest (scaled)
        #allYears[, t] <- pmax(0, N_after - current_h_vec)
        u_eff <- min(1, h / sum(N_after))  # cap at 100%
        H_vec <- u_eff * N_after * harvest_weights
        allYears[, t] <- pmax(0, N_after - H_vec)
      }

      # Store total population
      sim_results[[s]] <- colSums(allYears) * 2.56
    }

    # Convert to tidy data frame
    temp_df <- as.data.frame(sim_results)
    names(temp_df) <- paste0("V", 1:nSims)

    temp_df$Year <- 0:nYears
    temp_df$HarvestLevel <- as.factor(h)
    temp_df$Scenario <- scenario_name

    master_results[[as.character(h)]] <- temp_df |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = starts_with("V"),
        names_to = "SimID",
        values_to = "Population"
      )
  }
  master_results # Moved out of loop
}


#### Run without stochasticity
# 'stochastic_multiplier' is set to 1 if 'stoch' is FALSE, so then only the
# initialization of the number of females between 'Init_Min' and 'Init_Max'
# involves stochasticity, but not the progress from one year to another.
stoch <- FALSE

res_bfar <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = bfar_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                       nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,
                       K_females = K_females, SAD_Split = SAD_Split, harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                       scenario_name = "bfar")
res_dag <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = dag_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                            nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,
                            K_females = K_females, SAD_Split = SAD_Split, harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                            scenario_name = "dag")
res_adag <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = adag_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                           nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,
                           K_females = K_females, SAD_Split = SAD_Split, harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                           scenario_name = "adag")

res_all <- do.call(rbind, c(res_bfar, res_dag, res_adag))

# Set the order of the factor levels to determine the order of facets in the plot
res_all$Scenario <- factor(res_all$Scenario, levels = c("bfar", "dag", "adag"))
res_all$SimID <- factor(res_all$SimID, levels = paste0("V", seq_along(unique(res_all$SimID))))
head(res_all)
tail(res_all)
str(res_all)

ggplot(data = res_all,
       mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Population, col = SimID, group = SimID)) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(HarvestLevel), cols = vars(Scenario), labeller = label_both) +
  geom_point(size = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Population over time; stochasticity: ", stoch),
       caption = paste0("Colors show ", nSims, " different simulations")) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave(filename = paste0("res_all_stoch_", stoch,
                         format(Sys.time(), format = "%Y_%m_%d_%H_%M"), ".png"),
       width = 2000, height = 2000, units = "px", dpi = 300)
getwd() # See where the plot was saved


#### Run with stochasticity
# 'stochastic_multiplier' is set to 1 if 'stoch' is FALSE, so then only the
# initialization of the number of females between 'Init_Min' and 'Init_Max'
# involves stochasticity, but not the progress from one year to another.
stoch <- TRUE

res_bfar <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = bfar_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                            nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,

res_dag <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = dag_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                           nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,
                           K_females = K_females, SAD_Split = SAD_Split, harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                           scenario_name = "dag")
res_adag <- run_leslie_loop(base_mat = adag_mat, harvest_levels = harvest_levels, stoch = stoch,
                            nSims = nSims, nYears = nYears, Init_Min = Init_Min, Init_Max = Init_Max,
                            K_females = K_females, SAD_Split = SAD_Split, harvest_weights = harvest_weights,
                            scenario_name = "adag")

res_all <- do.call(rbind, c(res_bfar, res_dag, res_adag))

# Set the order of the factor levels to determine the order of facets in the plot
res_all$Scenario <- factor(res_all$Scenario, levels = c("bfar", "dag", "adag"))
res_all$SimID <- factor(res_all$SimID, levels = paste0("V", seq_along(unique(res_all$SimID))))
head(res_all)
tail(res_all)
str(res_all)

ggplot(data = res_all,
       mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Population, col = SimID, group = SimID)) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(HarvestLevel), cols = vars(Scenario), labeller = label_both) +
  geom_point(size = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Population over time; stochasticity: ", stoch),
       caption = paste0("Colors show ", nSims, " different simulations")) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave(filename = paste0("res_all_stoch_", stoch,
                         format(Sys.time(), format = "%Y_%m_%d_%H_%M"), ".png"),
       width = 2000, height = 2000, units = "px", dpi = 300)
getwd() # See where the plot was saved

Given these results, a good way to check the code is to see if you can reproduce known features. For example, it makes sense that if harvest_level increases, at some point the population cannot sustain itself and goes extinct, what indeed you observe. Similarly, bfar_mat is more like adag_mat than like dag_mat in that bfar_mat and adag_mat have the same adult survival rate, so you would expect the results of bfar_mat and adag_mat to be similar, what is also what you observe.

From the theory of Lesie matrices, you would also expect that the distribution of age classes tends to a distribution that can be calculated based on the Leslie matrix. If I understand it correctly, the distribution of the age classes is currently not returned by your function, but otherwise you could compare that distribution with the one you can calculate from the Leslie matrix.

For the results with stoch = TRUE, it seems that the stochasticity has a very large effect compared to the overall trend, so should you sample from a smaller distribution?

Q: Text Editor in C++ A:

I can't use containers (such as string, vector, etc. I mean I have to use pointers instead)

It would be better to use the standard library(which include std::vector etc) in C++. C and C++ are very different languages. Forget almost everything about C and treat C++ as a new language. This means to use std::vector etc. There's no real reason to avoid these since unless you're writing low level code and doing some microoptimization(which isn't recommended anyway).

Q: Access database from shared lib vs. microservice A:

Using shared database between different services is considered and antipattern in microservice architecture, though I would argue there are nuances there - in my current project we have a lot separate services working with the same database, the caveat is that basically it is the same service which is split into read and write view (basically CQRS-like approach) and our CI/CD pipeline is not that well suited to maintain such separation in a single solution with dependable deployment units (and adjusting it TBH does not worth the effort at the moment).

So the answer hugely depends on the context here. Anyway I would recommend against using nuget packages here cause it can quickly become a mess (from my personal experience) without basically any benefits.

If your situation is kind of similar to one I have described in my project - I would go with tightly coupled approach with maintaining the db schema in both services which will allow you to modify and deploy it in both separately (though you still will need to jump extra hoops to avoid breaking changes, for example when deleting a column you will need to remove code working with a column in both and deploy it and only after that you will be able to deploy migration deleting the column).

If both services perform write operations and you need to maintain some invariant then moving the database to a separate service looks like the best approach.

Also I would consider merging those 2 services into a single one - some times it is a viable approach too.

Q: Is it normal that std::unordered_map has different bucket_counts? A:

Yes, this is normal. Try to implement a bucket-based map from scratch, and you will see that there is some degree of arbitrariness in the way the set of keys is broken into buckets. This classification is based on the value of the hash code obtained from every key. Every time you get a new key and its hash code, you have to decide if you have to create a new bucket or add this key to an existing bucket closest by the hash code value. Note that at the moment of this decision, you don't know the total number of key-value pairs in the map during its lifetime. These decisions is a matter of optimization, so you have a trade-off between the complexity of this calculation and the optimization of the set of buckets. There is always a trade-off between redundancy (and, hence, memory usage) and performance.
(Note that two extremes, either exactly 1 bucket or the number of buckets equal to the number of keys would defeat the purpose of the algorithm, leading to the time complexity of O(N), that is, always the worst-case scenario possible for the bucket system. The optimal decision will be somewhere in between.)

I am not sure if you put any difference in your sample compared to the sample on this page, but the number of buckets can be implementation-dependent. Note the word possible in possible output.
